The High Priestly Prayer
PRAYR
noun phrase
From the Greek proseuchē, “prayer,” so called because in it Christ intercedes for His own as the great High Priest in the seventeenth chapter of John.

Biblical Definition

On the night before His passion, having finished His discourse, the Lord Jesus lifted up His eyes to heaven and prayed to His Father for Himself, for His apostles, and for all that should believe through their word (Joh 17). It is rightly called the high priestly prayer, for in it the great High Priest intercedes for His people before He goes to offer Himself for them. And the prayer is particular, not general: I pray for them, He saith; I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine (Joh 17:9). He prayed that the Father would keep them, sanctify them through the truth, and make them one; and He stretched the prayer beyond the eleven: Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word (Joh 17:20). The dictionary marks the high priestly prayer as the great pattern and proof of Christ’s particular intercession for His own. So the Scripture teaches that Christ ever liveth to make intercession, and that His intercession is for a definite people, the same the Father gave Him and for whom He died, and not for the world as such. As He prayed in that hour for them and not for the world, so He pleads now for the elect; and because His intercession is particular and prevailing, they whom He prays for are kept, sanctified, and brought at last to behold His glory.

Webster 1828 Definition

The prayer of John 17 in which Christ, as great High Priest, intercedes particularly for His own and not for the world.

expand to see more

THE HIGH PRIESTLY PRAYER, the prayer of Christ in the seventeenth chapter of John.

He prayed it on the night before His passion, lifting His eyes to heaven.

I pray not for the world, He said, but for them which thou hast given me.

He prayed also for all that should believe through the apostles’ word.

It is the great pattern of His particular and prevailing intercession.

Key Scripture

Joh 17:9 — "I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine."

Joh 17:20 — "Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word;"

Joh 17:24 — "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world."

Heb 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Modern Corruption

A prayer of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches His particular intercession for the people the Father gave Him.

expand to see more

The high priestly prayer has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the most solemn passages of the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the particular and prevailing intercession of Christ for His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the particular intercession of Christ for the people the Father gave Him. In that hour He said plainly, I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; His prayer was for a definite people, the same for whom He was about to die. So the Scripture teaches that Christ ever liveth to make intercession, and that His pleading at the Father’s right hand is for the elect, the very ones He redeemed. Because His intercession is particular and prevailing, they whom He prays for are kept, sanctified through the truth, made one, and brought at last to behold His glory; for the Son’s prayer is never refused of the Father.

Hebrew Roots

From the prayer of John 17, the name marks Christ’s priestly intercession for His own.
